extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; philosophers and educated general readers interested in metaphysics, religion, and theory-evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for assessing the plausibility, usefulness, and consistency of the metaphysical hypothesis of the Absolute (and competing pluralistic/theistic hypotheses). Focuses on intellectual, moral, aesthetic, pragmatic, and logical tests used in philosophical appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic: higher unity reconciles contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every higher total reconciles the contradictions which its parts, abstracted from it, prove implicitly to contain; two contradictory terms together engender a higher truth of which they both appear as indispensable members, mutually mediating aspects of that higher concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hegel's dialectic as an explanatory device when a synthesis plausibly absorbs and resolves apparent opposites. Empirical examples include: peace secured by armaments, liberty by laws, simplicity achieved by artificial training, and domestication reconciling will to live with will to kill. Anti-pattern: treating the dialectic as an automatic proof rather than an interpretive schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalist demand for an absolute, self-securing truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalism postulates a truth that is universal, single, indivisible, eternal, objective, and necessary — a truth which 'must be' rather than merely 'may be' and which secures itself by incorporating or negating its possible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims according to whether they purport to be self-securing (contain their own negations) and whether that device is legitimately established rather than rhetorically imposed. Note the method of 'double negation' as the rationalist device for self-security. Anti-pattern: accepting 'must-be' pronouncements without scrutiny of their justificatory basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious intellectualism (conceptual exclusion as denial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of assuming that a concept excludes from any reality conceived by its means everything not included in the concept's definition — treating an abstract concept as if it were a denial of all else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conceptual definitions cautiously: don't infer ontological negations merely from conceptual exclusion. Recognize that intellectualistic treatment can produce spurious contradictions and force artificial triadic progressions. Anti-pattern: using conceptual exclusion to claim that any particular thing's concept entails the non-existence of everything else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold dimensions of rationality for evaluating hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationality has at least four dimensions — intellectual, aesthetical, moral, and practical — and a satisfactory hypothesis should be appraised across all these respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a metaphysical or philosophical hypothesis, assess how it performs in each dimension: e.g., mechanical materialism may be intellectually rational (calculable) but aesthetically ugly and morally barren; theistic views may be morally satisfying but frustrating intellectually; political/practical rationality may conflict with moral/aesthetic demands. Avoid assessing truth solely on one dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance-of-rationality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the conception which yields the largest overall 'balance' of rationality across the various dimensions, rather than demanding perfect rationality in every respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh gains and losses across intellectual, aesthetic, moral, and practical values; select the hypothesis that maximizes net rational plausibility. Anti-pattern: privileging perfection in one dimension while ignoring severe deficits in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/aesthetic weight in hypothesis appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional value (peace, sublimity) and aesthetic effects are legitimate factors that weight the credit side of a metaphysical hypothesis — e.g., the absolute confers a certain peace that counts for something in its favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include affective and aesthetic consequences among the pragmatic reasons for belief, acknowledging that such values can make an otherwise poorly evidenced hypothesis attractive. Guidance: do not let emotional weight substitute for logical or empirical adequacy, but do count it in the overall balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency requirement for wholes and their parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideally perfect whole should be the whole of which the parts also are perfect; if a theory defines an 'ideal' whole whose parts are manifestly imperfect, that signals internal inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test claims about totalities by examining whether their parts meet the standard the theory sets for the whole. Example: absolutism defines an ideally perfect whole, yet its parts (finite experiences) are imperfect — this undermines the conception's internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of evil and error as a decisive test
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphysical theory must account for the existence of evil and error; absolutism faces a speculative 'problem of evil' because a perfect, all-inclusive absolute seemingly requires or contains particular hideous forms of life and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a theory explains the presence and role of suffering and error without incoherence. Anti-pattern: invoking the absolute's 'overcoming' of evil without explaining why the absolute would contain or require such particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective vs prospective explanatory power (usefulness for deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute is criticized as 'useless for deductive purposes' because it functions retrospectively (it can adopt details after the fact) and does not enable prior naming or prediction of phenomenal details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that have prospective, predictive, or deductive utility in navigating experience and informing action. A theory that only accounts for events after they occur is pragmatically weaker for guiding inquiry and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony and practical plausibility regarding cognitive burden
rubrics_metrics.description: An idealistic absolute that must be explicitly aware of all negations and every particular fact carries an implausible burden of 'unprofitable information' — making the conception practically and cognitively extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply parsimony and consider the implausibility of positing entities or structures that require infinite, explicit, and useless content. Anti-pattern: accepting metaphysical posits that force enormous explanatory baggage without payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the absolute from a finite personal God
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the metaphysical Absolute (the all-inclusive monist/pantheist whole) with the finite, personal God of ordinary religion; they are different hypotheses with different implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious claims, keep clear which hypothesis is under consideration: a finite God who exists within a pluralistic system has different moral, practical, and theological consequences than an absolute that contains everything. Avoid equivocation between these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical moral test offered by pluralistic metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: In pluralistic metaphysics, the problems that evil presents become practical (how to lessen evil) rather than speculative puzzles; such metaphysics may thus have an advantage in guiding moral action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor metaphysical views that translate into actionable moral guidance and practical responses to suffering, rather than those that ground only speculative explanations. Assess theories by their capacity to inform ethical practice and problem-solving.
